Derision is the feeling or act of thinking someone or something is completely ridiculous and worthless — and showing it, often by laughing at them, mocking them, or treating them with contempt.

It is not just a private feeling of amusement. Derision is expressed outward. The person doing it wants the target to know they are being looked down upon. It is scornful, dismissive laughter — the kind that is meant to humiliate, not to share joy.

Think of it this way: when you laugh with someone, that is warmth. When you laugh at someone in a way that says "you are pathetic and beneath me," that is derision.

Derision sits at the crossroads of mockery + contempt + dismissiveness. Let us look at each ingredient:

  • Mockery — you are making fun of someone, imitating them, or ridiculing their ideas.
  • Contempt — you do not just find them funny; you actually look down on them. You consider them beneath serious attention.
  • Dismissiveness — you refuse to take them seriously at all. Their ideas, efforts, or worth are treated as laughable, not worth engaging with.

When all three combine, you get derision. It is one of the harshest social responses a person can receive, because it does not just say "I disagree with you" — it says "you are not even worth disagreeing with seriously."
What Derision Looks Like in Real Life

Derision shows up in many forms:

  • A crowd bursting into laughter when someone presents an idea they find absurd.
  • Someone letting out a sharp, scornful laugh — a "Ha!" — at a suggestion they find ridiculous.
  • People rolling their eyes and smirking at someone who is speaking.
  • A sneering tone of voice that signals: "I cannot believe you even said that."
  • An audience jeering and booing a performer off stage.

All of these carry the same DNA: you are ridiculous, and I want you to know it.

These sentences will show you exactly how the word is used in context:

"When he proposed his new business idea, he was met with derision from the entire board of directors."

(The board laughed at him and dismissed him scornfully — they did not take him seriously at all.)

"She held her rival's efforts in derision, calling the work amateurish and embarrassing."

(She looked down on her rival's work with mocking contempt.)

"Despite the public derision he faced, the scientist continued his research — and was eventually proven right."

(The public mocked and ridiculed him, but he persisted.)

"His voice was full of derision as he read aloud from the letter, making everyone laugh at its contents."

(His tone was scornful and mocking as he read it.)

You will often see derision paired with these:

  • "met with derision" — when a person's idea, action, or appearance is greeted with mockery by others.
  • "held in derision" — when someone is continuously regarded as ridiculous, over a period of time.
  • "object of derision" — the person or thing being mocked and laughed at. ("He became the object of derision after the incident.")
  • "greeted with derision" — similar to "met with," it signals that the immediate response to something was scorn and mockery.
  • "derision in someone's voice/eyes/laugh" — describing the quality of someone's expression when they are mocking.
Intensity: Where Does Derision Sit on the Scale?

It helps to understand derision relative to words that are close to it in meaning:

  • Teasing — light, often affectionate poking fun. Not necessarily unkind. Low intensity.
  • Mockery — deliberately making fun of someone in a way that hurts. Unkind. Medium intensity.
  • Ridicule — aggressive mocking, meant to make someone look foolish. High intensity.
  • Derision — all of the above, plus a layer of deep contempt and dismissal. The person is not just mocked — they are considered utterly beneath serious respect. Very high intensity.

Derision is not playful. It is cold, scornful, and often cruel.
An Important Nuance: Who Feels Derision vs. Who Experiences It?

• The person showing derision feels superiority, scorn, and contempt. They find the target laughable.
  • The person receiving derision typically feels humiliated, belittled, and dismissed.

This is what makes derision so sharp as a social weapon — it attacks not just someone's idea or action, but their entire credibility and dignity.
One Final Way to Remember It

Imagine you worked very hard on a painting and showed it to a crowd. Instead of applause or even polite silence, the crowd bursts into mocking laughter, people point and sneer, and someone shouts "Did a child draw this?"

That response — that scornful, contemptuous, humiliating laughter — is derision. And the crowd's laughter would be described as a laugh of derision, or you would say your work was met with derision.

It is one of the most cutting responses a person can face — because it does not even offer the dignity of being taken seriously.
